prompt.context: Tuck Health is a non-profit integrated health care system based in Texas and New Mexico. Integrated health care systems include hospitals, philanthropic organizations, nursing homes, senior resident facilities, physician clinics, outpatient surgeries and diagnostic centers, and community outreach programs. The CEO wants to grow the organization.
prompt.question: The CEO wants to grow the organization. How would you say he can achieve this goal? This is a structured case with multiple sub-questions that will be asked sequentially.

clarifying_info.q: What does growth mean for a non-profit organization?
clarifying_info.a: Growth means service quality, fairness, and reach — but in this case the CEO most importantly wants to achieve profitability and increase in size.

clarifying_info.q: Is this case focused on one specific aspect of growth or the overall strategy?
clarifying_info.a: This is a McKinsey-style structured case covering growth strategy, capacity decisions, physician employment strategy, and profitability analysis across multiple sequential questions.

framework: Growth avenues: New Services, New Markets, New Channels
Growth mechanisms: Joint Venture, Acquisition, or Organic growth
Key influencers: Doctors/physicians who send patients to the hospitals
Non-profit considerations: Core mission (service quality, fairness, reach) must align with profitability goals
Profitability levers: Revenue side (volume, price, service mix) and Cost side (fixed vs. variable)

questions.prompt: Q1: The CEO wants to grow the organization. How would you say he can achieve this goal? What does growth mean for a non-profit?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize growth for a non-profit spans mission and financial dimensions. Strong answer covers: (1) Non-profit growth = service quality, fairness, reach — not just profit. (2) Three growth vectors: New Services, New Markets, New Channels. (3) Three mechanisms to achieve growth: JV, acquisition, or organic. (4) Critical insight: key influencers are the doctors/physicians who refer patients to hospitals — candidate should proactively identify this.

questions.prompt: Q2: The CEO is considering adding additional capacity. What factors would you want him to consider before investing?
questions.guidance: Strong answer should be MECE and cover: Demand factors (how much extra demand exists, how sustainable, how much to capture, competitor reaction); Time horizon (how long to capture demand); Resource constraints (access to capital, required ROI, profit margins, space/labor availability); Availability of alternatives (acquisition targets); Non-profit lens (does it affect core mission goals).

questions.prompt: Q3: A few years back, Tuck Health adopted a strategy of employing physician practices to grow the system. How would you evaluate whether this strategy has achieved success?
questions.guidance: Candidate should evaluate success across three stakeholder groups. Hospitals: profitability improvement, patient volume growth. Patients: service quality/flexibility (better care), better reach, fair access, integrated services. Physicians: compensation benchmark (before vs. after joining), physician satisfaction (lifestyle, value-added services). Strong answer frames metrics for each stakeholder and proposes before-vs-after comparison methodology.

questions.prompt: Q4: Tuck Health was formed by the merger of two IHS systems — one in Texas and one in New Mexico. Texas has seen rapid growth from the physician employment strategy, but New Mexico has not. What could have caused this disparity? (Note: cost side is the same for both.)
questions.guidance: Since costs are equal, focus the analysis on the revenue/demand side. Macro factors: market growth rate, market size, age and health of population, per capita income. Competition: competitive intensity, market structure. Micro factors: management quality, service mix differences, price mix differences, geographic location differences. Strong candidate quickly narrows to macro market factors and competitive structure as most likely root causes.

questions.prompt: Q5: Describe what referrals are and explain ways to determine whether physician growth has resulted in facility/hospital growth.
questions.guidance: Referrals = physicians directing patients to specific hospitals/facilities for procedures, tests, or specialist care. Methods to measure impact: (1) Simple correlation — does increase in employed physicians correspond to facility patient volume growth? (2) Profile individual physicians and track their referral patterns before vs. after joining the system. Strong candidate anticipates the before/after analysis and proactively raises potential confounding factors.

questions.prompt: Q6: What would you worry about when doing a before/after referral analysis on physicians who joined the system?
questions.guidance: Key concern is isolating the effect of hiring physicians from external factors. Confounding variables to flag: addition of new capacity (could independently drive volume), addition of new services, changes in market structure, changes in competitive structure, changes in cost/pricing structure. Strong answer frames this as a causal inference problem — the goal is to isolate physician hiring as the cause of patient growth, controlling for all other factors.

questions.prompt: Q7: Using the following data and a 5-year horizon, would you recommend the CEO continue employing physicians? CM per new patient = $10,000. One-time new physician investment = $900K per physician. Data table: Markets with no physicians = 1,000 new patients; Markets with no new physicians added (existing: 100 physicians) = 2,000 new patients; Markets with new physicians added (existing: 50, new: 50 physicians) = 4,000 new patients.
questions.guidance: Candidate must identify the incremental patients attributable to new physicians, calculate total CM, compare against investment. Key steps: calculate incremental patients from adding physicians, multiply by CM per patient, sum over 5 years, compare to total one-time investment. Arrive at NPV conclusion (approximately breakeven / NPV ≈ 0), then overlay strategic considerations for recommendation.

math.setup: Incremental patients from new physicians = patients in markets with new physicians added minus patients in comparable markets without new physicians. Investment = 50 new physicians × $900K each.
steps: Incremental patients attributable to new physicians: 4,000 (markets with new physicians) − 2,000 (markets with no new physicians added) = 2,000 incremental new patients
Annual CM from incremental patients: 2,000 patients × $10,000 CM = $20,000,000 per year
Undiscounted return: $100M revenue vs $45M investment — positive. However accounting for discount rate and cost of capital, NPV ≈ 0 (breakeven on purely financial basis).
math.answer: NPV ≈ $0 (breakeven). The strategy pays for itself financially over 5 years but does not generate significant excess returns.

questions.prompt: Q8: What is your final recommendation to the CEO regarding the physician employment strategy?
questions.guidance: Strong recommendation integrates financial and strategic dimensions. Financial: NPV ≈ 0 means the strategy is financially neutral — does not destroy value. Strategic: the strategy achieves important non-financial growth goals (reach, more services, better care). Focus recommendation: concentrate resources on high-growth Texas market where the strategy has proven effective. For New Mexico: gather more information before committing (market type, physician count, total addressable patients). Risks to flag: physician integration challenges, cost overruns, market saturation.

brainstorming.prompt: What are all the factors that could explain why the physician employment strategy succeeded in Texas but not in New Mexico?

categories.name: Market Macro Factors
ideas: Higher population growth rate in Texas vs. New Mexico
Larger addressable patient population in Texas
Younger/healthier population in New Mexico reducing healthcare demand
Higher per capita income in Texas enabling more elective procedures

categories.name: Competitive Dynamics
ideas: More fragmented physician market in Texas making acquisition easier
Stronger incumbent competitors in New Mexico
Existing hospital systems with locked-in referral relationships in New Mexico

categories.name: Micro/Internal Factors
ideas: Stronger management execution in Texas division
Different service mix offered in each market
Different pricing strategies or reimbursement rates
Location of acquired practices (urban vs. rural)
Quality of physicians acquired in each market

categories.name: Integration Factors
ideas: Cultural differences between acquired practices and Tuck Health
Physician satisfaction and retention differences post-acquisition
Speed of integration and system adoption
Alignment of incentives in employment contracts

recommendation: Proceed with physician employment strategy in Texas where NPV ≈ 0 and non-financial growth goals (reach, services, quality) are being achieved
Hold expansion in New Mexico pending further analysis of market conditions, competitive structure, and physician availability
risks: Financial risk: NPV is approximately breakeven — any cost overruns or lower-than-expected patient volumes would make the strategy value-destructive
Integration risk: employed physicians may not refer at expected rates if not properly incentivized or satisfied
Market risk: competitive response from other healthcare systems could erode incremental patient capture
next_steps: Gather New Mexico market data: market size, growth rate, competitive dynamics, number of available physicians to hire
Conduct physician satisfaction analysis in Texas to understand success drivers replicable in New Mexico
Define clear NPV hurdle rate and monitoring metrics (referral rates, patient volumes, CM per physician) with 12-month review checkpoint
